In 1910, the Women's Trade Union League (WTLU) of Massachusetts, under the leadership of Elizabeth Evans, took up the cause of minimum wage legislation in Massachusetts.
The 1910 effort was in conjunction with advocacy work led by Florence Kelley of the National Consumer League.
Over the next two years, a coalition of social reform groups and labor advocates in Boston pushed for minimum wage legislation in the state.
In 1912, Massachusetts passed the first American minimum wage legislation.

Within eight years, at least thirteen U.S. states and the District of Columbia would pass minimum wage laws.

The United States Supreme Court of the Lochner era consistently invalidated compulsory minimum wage laws.

Muller v. Oregon upheld maximum working hours laws for women on the grounds that women required special protection that men did not.
